newsitem.title: UK: New UK Chancellor kickstarts gilt options trade.
newsitem.headline: New UK Chancellor kickstarts gilt options trade.

text.p: Gilt options trade sprang into action on Tuesday after Britain's new Chancellor of the Exchequer raised interest rates and surprised markets with plans to give the Bank of England more independence.
Implied volatility of front month gilt options soared around a full point and volumes swelled, sparking activity in a market that took Labour's landslide election victory in its stride.
"It feels like a dam has burst," said a trader at a French brokerage on the LIFFE floor. "Volatility has taken a jump, and activity has bounded."

Earlier, Chancellor Gordon Brown announced a quarter point rise in interest rates to 6.25 percent, and gave the Bank of England responsibility for setting interest rates. The inflation target will still be laid down by the Treasury.
On Tuesday, after opening weaker, implied volatility of June options shot to 8.0 percent, compared with 7.25 percent on Thursday and 7.0 percent at the open.

In the six week runup to the election, many traders at the London International Financial Futures and Options Exchange were surprised how calmly the market was reacting to the expected end of 18 years of Conservative power.
June volatility had headed back to the 7.0 percent level on Friday, more than reversing its limited 50 basis point rise to 8.50 percent on election day on Thursday.
Volatility was well below the 10.0 percent registered ahead of the last election in 1992.
September options on the September gilt futures rose to 7.65 percent, after opening around 7.39 percent, and some traders said they expected it to head to 8.0 percent.

"It's not as high as I expected, and I feel there's more to come once the underlying (futures) have calmed a bit," said a salesman at a European bank in London. "We're seeing a lot of trade going through."
More than 22,000 June calls had changed hands by 1315 GMT.
June gilt futures were up 1-29/32 at 113-00, after setting a new contract high of 113-24 earlier.
Andy Ash, derivatives analyst at Monument Derivatives said the speed of the rise in gilt futures had wrong-footed many traders after they had sold June call options last week.
"Aggressive buying of the 112 calls left the pit short gamma," he said. "People had to struggle to cover it, which bid up the vol."
Gamma is the measure of the rate of change in the value of an option, compared with the rate of change in the underlying future.
Ash said volatility was a sell around the 8.0 percent level, as the downside potential for gilts was not sufficiently strong to support the uptick in volatility.
Norman Beauchamp, head of derivatives at Cooperative Bank in London said the progress towards independence for the BoE was a very pro-Europe move, and as such would maintain the underlying gilt rise.
"Europe is the key issue," said Beauchamp. "The spread over Bunds has collapsed to 140 basis points from 180 before the election and gilts are still a buy."
